# Introduction

This project analyses TikTok data to better understand video performance and user viewing behaviour.

The analysis combines several perspectives on the platform, including video performance, feed impressions, user preferences, session behaviour, and watch events. In addition, regression analysis is used to examine whether characteristics of TikTok impressions are associated with the amount of time users spend watching content.

The separate analyses are combined in this final report to provide an overview of the main patterns found in the TikTok data.

# Data Inspection

## Loading the data

The video-view data are accessed through the SQLite database to demonstrate how project data can be retrieved from a database.

The cleaned datasets generated by the individual analyses are stored in the `data/processed/` folder.

```{r}
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)

# Video-view data from SQLite
con <- dbConnect(
  SQLite(),
  here("data", "raw", "tiktok_students.sqlite")
)

views <- dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT * FROM video_view"
)

dbDisconnect(con)

impressions <- read.csv(
  here("data", "processed", "impressions_clean.csv")
)

sessions <- read.csv(
  here("data", "processed", "sessions_clean.csv")
)

users <- read.csv(
  here("data", "processed", "users_clean.csv")
)

watch_events <- read.csv(
  here("data", "processed", "watch_events_clean.csv")
)
```


## Video-view dataset overview

The video-view dataset contains information about TikTok videos, including video length, impressions, watched views, creators, and watch rate.

```{r}
dim(views)
head(views)
colSums(is.na(views))
```

## Impression dataset overview

The impression dataset contains information about individual impressions, including user and content characteristics.

```{r}
dim(impressions)
head(impressions)
colSums(is.na(impressions))
```

## Watch-event dataset overview

The watch-event data contain information about users' watching behaviour.

```{r}
dim(watch_events)
head(watch_events)
colSums(is.na(watch_events))
```

## Users dataset overview

The user dataset contains user-level characteristics, including baseline usage behaviour, interaction tendencies, and preferences for different content categories.
```{r}
dim(users)
head(users)
colSums(is.na(users))
```

## Sessions dataset overview

The session dataset contains information about individual Tiktok sessions, including session duration, number of videos viewed, total watch time, and the user associated with each session.
```{r}
dim(sessions)
head(sessions)
colSums(is.na(sessions))
```

# Descriptive Analysis

## Overall video performance

We first calculate several overall performance measures for the video-view dataset.

```{r}
overview <- views %>%
  summarise(
    videos = n(),
    creators = n_distinct(creator_id),
    avg_length = mean(video_length_sec, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_impressions = mean(impressions_n, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_watched = mean(watched_n, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_watch_rate = mean(watch_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_watch_share = mean(
      watched_n / impressions_n,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    avg_watch_seconds = mean(
      video_length_sec * watched_n / impressions_n,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

overview
```

This provides an overall picture of the number of videos and creators in the dataset, as well as average reach and watching behaviour.

## Watch share

To examine the proportion of impressions that resulted in a watched view, we calculate watch share as a percentage.

```{r}
views <- views %>%
  mutate(
    watched_pct = watched_n / impressions_n * 100
  )

head(views)
```

Watch share provides a measure of how much of the observed audience proceeded to watch the video.

## Most viewed video

The video with the highest number of impressions is identified below.

```{r}
topvideo <- views %>%
  filter(
    impressions_n == max(
      impressions_n,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

topvideo
```

This identifies the video that achieved the highest observed reach in the dataset.

## Distribution of video length

The distribution of video length is visualised using a histogram.

```{r}
hist(
  views$video_length_sec,
  main = "Distribution of Video Length",
  xlab = "Video length (seconds)"
)
```

The distribution provides an overview of the typical length of videos in the dataset and whether particularly short or long videos are common.

## Videos with high watch rates

We identify videos with a watch rate above 80%.

```{r}
goodvideos <- views %>%
  filter(
    watch_rate > 0.8
  )

nrow(goodvideos)
```

This shows how many videos achieved a relatively high watch rate according to the threshold used in the analysis.

## Top 10 videos by watch rate

The ten videos with the highest watch rates are displayed below.

```{r}
top_watch_rate <- views %>%
  select(
    video_id,
    creator_id,
    impressions_n,
    watched_n,
    watch_rate
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    desc(watch_rate)
  ) %>%
  slice_head(
    n = 10
  )

top_watch_rate
```

This allows the videos with the strongest observed watch rates to be compared.

## Performance by creator

Video performance is also aggregated at the creator level.

```{r}
creator_summary <- views %>%
  group_by(creator_id) %>%
  summarise(
    videos = n(),
    total_impressions = sum(
      impressions_n,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    average_watch_rate = mean(
      watch_rate,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    desc(total_impressions)
  )

creator_summary
```

This comparison provides insight into differences in reach and average watch rate between creators.

# Regression Analysis

The regression analysis investigates whether characteristics of Tiktok impressions are associated with the amount of time users spend watching the content. 

The dependent variable in all three models is `watch_seconds`. The regression models and figures are created in `Regression.R`.

```{r}
#| include: false

invisible(capture.output(source(here("src", "Regression.R"))))
```

## Simple regression

The first model examines the whether the overall Tiktok score,`score_total` is associated with watch time.

```{r}
summary(model1)
```

This model provides the baseline association between the total score and watch time without controlling for the other variables.

## Multiple regression

The second model adds additional explanatory variables:

- `feed_rank`
- `score_category_match`
- `score_creator_match`
- `score_satiation_penalty`
- `source_bucket`

```{r}
summary(model2)
```

The multiple regression allows the association between `score_total` and watch time changes after accounting for these additional characteristics. 

## User fixed effects

The third model additionally controls for differences between users by including `user_id` as a fixed effect.

```{r}
summary(model3)
```

Including `user_id` controls for systematic differences between users that could otherwise be associated with differences in watch time.

## Recommendation score and watch time

The figure below visualizes the relationship between the overall recommendation score and watch time.

# Conclusions

The regression analysis examined whether a higher TikTok recommendation score was associated with longer watch time.

In Model 1, `score_total` was not significantly associated with watch time (`p = 0.385`).

After additional recommendation characteristics were included in Model 2, the coefficient for `score_total` became positive but remained just above the conventional 5% significance threshold (`p = 0.0501`). `score_category_match` showed a statistically significant negative association with watch time.

After controlling for differences between users in Model 3, the relationship between `score_total` and watch time remained statistically uncertain (`p = 0.071`). The negative association for `score_category_match` remained statistically significant.

Overall, the models provide limited evidence that the overall recommendation score is associated with watch time. The final model explained approximately 0.8% of the variation in watch time, suggesting that much of the variation is associated with factors not captured by these models.

These findings describe associations and should not be interpreted as causal effects.

# Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the results.

First, the analysis is based on observational data. Therefore, the regression models identify associations but cannot by themselves establish causal relationships.

Second, the models only include the variables available in the datasets. Other characteristics of users, videos, or the recommendation system may influence watch behaviour but are not necessarily captured in the models.

Third, the results of the regression analysis depend on the specification of the models. Different variables, transformations, or model specifications could lead to different estimates.

Finally, the user fixed-effects specification controls for differences between users, but it does not eliminate all potential sources of omitted-variable bias or establish causality.

# Overall Conclusion

Overall, the project provides a broad overview of TikTok video performance and user viewing behaviour.

The descriptive video analysis highlights differences in reach, watch rates, and creator performance. The impression analysis examines content delivery and ranking patterns, while the session analysis provides insight into session duration, videos viewed, watch time, and differences in activity across users. The user analysis highlights differences in content preferences, and the watch-event analysis shows how users respond to videos and how watch behaviour relates to video length.

The regression analysis provides a more structured examination of whether recommendation characteristics are associated with watch time. The results do not provide strong evidence that the overall recommendation score is clearly associated with longer watch time, while some individual recommendation components show associations with viewing behaviour.

Overall, the project demonstrates how multiple TikTok datasets can be cleaned, combined, analysed, visualised, and incorporated into one reproducible workflow. The findings should be interpreted as patterns and associations in the observed data rather than as causal effects.
